transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-25
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Matt Liang (Harborview CTO), Sara Gomez (Lead ML Eng), Evan Brooks (Infra), Leah Park (Product)

Summary:
Harborview is evaluating an exit from their current OpenAI-hosted stack toward a combination of Redwood Hosted (initial), then Dedicated or Private for regulated workloads. Main concerns: eval parity (responses & hallucination rates), vLLM/TGI runtime compatibility for local dev parity, 99th percentile latency targets, quantization effects on quality, and enterprise compliance (SOC2, KMS, SSO). Agreed next steps: Redwood to provide compatibility checklist, pricing/pilot template, customer to share sample prompts and infra details for a parity run.

Topics discussed:
- Migration drivers: cost & latency predictability, vendor lock-in escape hatch
- Runtime stack: vLLM/TGI parity and quantized model behavior
- Hosting options and SLA tradeoffs (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private VPC)
- Security/compliance: SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM, audit logs, data residency
- Benchmarks: token-level cost, p95/p99 latency, regen rates

[00:00] Alex Reed: Hey everybody, thanks for joining — quick intros?
[00:08] Matt Liang: Yup, Matt here, CTO at Harborview. We're looking at a port-out from our current provider, mainly cost creep and some latency tail issues.
[00:15] Alex Reed: Great — I'm Alex (AE), this is Priya (SE). We usually pair on these to cover product + technical fit.
[00:22] Priya Shah: Hi all — excited to dig in; quick clarifying q: are you aiming to run exactly the same inference stack (vLLM/TGI) in-house or move to Redwood hosted first?
[00:33] Sara Gomez: Good question — short term we want hosted to drop immediate costs, but long term we need Dedicated or Private because of PHI and our security policy. We also have a local vLLM-based dev flow and want eval parity vs what we've been getting from OpenAI.
[00:46] Evan Brooks: And we have firewall rules and strict egress, so Private VPC is likely a requirement for some teams.

[01:05] Priya Shah: Cool — typical path we see is hosted for fast test pilots, then Dedicated reserved pools, and Private for air-gapped or strict residency. For vLLM/TGI parity — we have a compatibility checklist that maps model artifacts, tokenizer quirks, kv cache handling and quantization differences.
[01:25] Matt Liang: That sounds useful. Our engineering leads say some prompts behaved differently when they ran a quantized Llama variant on vLLM vs responses from the hosted provider, so parity's the main blocker.
[01:38] Priya Shah: Totally. A couple things we look at: 1) model byte-for-byte equivalence and tokenization, 2) kernel/runtime differences (we sometimes see small beam differences because of attention kernel selection), 3) KV cache handling — vLLM's cache behavior and Redwood's runtime may treat prefix caching differently which affects regen.
[01:58] Sara Gomez: Can you give a concrete example of where it diverges?
[02:03] Priya Shah: Sure — we had a customer report the model answered differently when we applied a 4-bit quant profile: numbers in tables had rounding noise, so for exact-recall prompts the CITI… uh sorry, city names were swapped occasionally. Also TGI's sampling defaults vs our runtime sampling annealing differ and that affects fingerprint in narrow prompts.
[02:30] Leah Park: So for evaluation parity, are you recommending we run the same quantization locally or use Redwood's recommended quant?
[02:36] Priya Shah: Ideally both. We'll provide suggested quant config that balances size/cost and quality, plus a script to reproduce our inference settings. We'll also run a parity eval on your sample prompts to surface delta metrics — pass/fail thresholds you set (e.g., >95% intent match, <2% hallucination on fact-check set).
[02:57] Matt Liang: About latency — we have a p99 SLO at 500ms for our chat prod. Can Redwood meet that on Hosted?
[03:04] Alex Reed: Hosted can meet low-latency for many workloads; depends on sequence length and batching. For chat-like short-turns, typical p95 is ~120-200ms on our verified Llama-variants at default configs. p99 can spike with cold KV caches. For guaranteed p99 you'd want Dedicated with pinned capacity and pre-warmed KV caches.
[03:29] Evan Brooks: Do you have numbers for throughput on Dedicated and how autoscaling affects SLOs? We need to understand burst handling and fallback when a node is down.
[03:37] Priya Shah: Dedicated gives predictable throughput; we expose autoscale policies and burst lanes. In productions we recommend headroom of ~30% for spiky traffic, and automatic fallback to a lower-cost variant or a regional replica if capacity is constrained. We also have circuit-breaker policies so requests don't queue indefinitely.
[03:56] Sara Gomez: What about token-level accounting? Our finance team needs to know cost per 1k tokens and how caching affects it.
[04:02] Alex Reed: We provide token-level breakdown by route and model. Caching reduces billed tokens effectively — prefix caching can shave repeated context by 20–60% depending on app pattern. We'll share a sample cost model spreadsheet after the call.
[04:15] Matt Liang: On security: SOC2 is table stakes. We also need SSO via SAML and KMS-managed keys for private deployments. Can you go through your Private options?
[04:25] Priya Shah: For Private we offer a customer-controlled control plane with optional on-prem agent or VPC peering. KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, HSM) are available; audit logs retained per contract. SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported. We'll send SOC2 and our security pack.
[04:41] Leah Park: Any gotchas when moving from OpenAI — licensing, model artifacts?
[04:46] Priya Shah: Mostly around model weights and tokenizers; if you're using OpenAI proprietary endpoints, you can't export weights directly. For open models it's straightforward. We can run a parity eval with proxies that call their API (if allowed) to compare output. Also note small differences can come from sampling RNG seeds and compilation kernels.
[05:06] Matt Liang: We also use Anthropic for some tasks; mixing providers is part of our redundancy plan. Does Redwood support multi-model routing?
[05:14] Alex Reed: Yes — smart routing lets you route by policy (latency, cost, region). You can have a primary model and a fallback (Anthropic/OpenAI) for specific routes. That helps with graceful degradation.
[05:26] Evan Brooks: Network wise, for Private VPC we need to expose minimal egress. How do you handle peering and firewall openings?
[05:33] Priya Shah: We'll provide a network runbook — CIDR ranges, DNS, egress ports. For on-prem air-gapped installs we use an appliance and async sync for telemetry; for VPC peering we use private links. We'll ask for your infra diagram as an action item.
[05:50] Sara Gomez: For the parity run, what data do you need from us?
[05:53] Priya Shah: 3–5 representative prompt templates, a token distribution CSV, target metrics (intent match, hallucination tolerance), and any deterministic seeds if you have them. We'll run against your sample on both vLLM/TGI settings and our hosted runtime and produce a diff report with example off-cases.
[06:12] Alex Reed: To recap next steps — Priya will send the compatibility checklist and suggested quant configs; Alex will follow up with pricing and pilot contract; Harborview will share prompts and infra diagram. Plan to reconvene early December for Dedicated sizing demo.
[06:27] Matt Liang: Sounds good. Any immediate blockers from your side?
[06:30] Priya Shah: None — just access to the sample prompts and a permissive parity license if we need to call your current hosted provider for ground-truth.
[06:39] Leah Park: We'll confirm with legal on that.
[06:42] Matt Liang: Cool — thanks Alex, Priya.
[06:45] Alex Reed: Thanks everyone. I'll send the calendar invite for the follow-up.

End of transcript.
